decisions.title: Build a browser-only prototype first
decisions.problem: The team needed a working, demonstrable parent–teacher app quickly, covering many features, for a technopreneurship pitch.
alternatives: Build a backend and database from the start
decisions.decision: Keep all logic in the React app, seed it with realistic sample data, and save key records in browser storage so the demo survives a refresh.
tradeoffs: Very fast to build and easy to demo, with no server to run
Data stays on one device, so parents and teachers cannot share it in real time
Security is simulated: sign-in matches accounts in browser storage without verifying passwords, so a production version needs a backend with real authentication
evidence: App.tsx holds the app's data in 35 useState hooks
Three localStorage keys: schoolfam_users, schoolfam_roster, schoolfam_referral_codes
No network calls other than the Gemini API

decisions.title: Drive role access from one navigation list
decisions.problem: Four kinds of users (parents, teachers, admins and the super admin) need different screens, and hard-coding checks in every screen would be easy to get wrong.
alternatives: Separate apps or layouts per role
decisions.decision: Each menu item declares the roles that may see it, and the layout filters the list for the signed-in user.
tradeoffs: Access rules are easy to read and change in one place
In a browser-only app this hides screens but cannot protect data; a backend would need to enforce the same rules
evidence: components/Layout.tsx: 17 menu items, each with a roles list or 'all'
Classes is limited to admins; Homework, Moments and Health to teachers and parents

decisions.title: Use codes to control who can join
decisions.problem: Anyone could otherwise sign up as a teacher, or as the parent of any child.
alternatives: Open sign-up with manual approval by an admin
decisions.decision: Teachers need a staff ID or an active, single-use invite for the teacher role; parents need the access code of their child.
tradeoffs: Simple for schools to hand out on paper or by message
Codes are checked in the browser in this prototype; the super admin sign-up uses a key stored in the front-end code, which should move to a server before real use
evidence: Invite codes are marked 'used' after a successful sign-up
Parent sign-up looks up Child.accessCode in the class roster

decisions.title: Summarise a child's day with AI
decisions.problem: Teachers record many small activities a day; parents want a quick, warm overview and something to talk about at home.
alternatives: Show the raw activity list only
decisions.decision: Send the child's class and the day's activities to gemini-2.5-flash with a structured prompt (skills, mood, a conversation starter) and render the Markdown reply.
tradeoffs: Personal, readable summaries with little extra work for teachers
The API key is injected into the browser build, so it is visible to users; a production version should call Gemini through a server
AI output needs review because the mood observation is inferred
evidence: services/geminiService.ts builds the prompt and calls gemini-2.5-flash
vite.config.ts injects GEMINI_API_KEY at build time
Friendly fallback messages when the key is missing or the request fails

decisions.title: Model every feature with TypeScript types
decisions.problem: With 21 feature screens sharing data, mismatched field names or invalid statuses would cause hard-to-find bugs.
decisions.decision: Define every record as a TypeScript interface, with union types for statuses such as invoice, pickup and feedback states.
tradeoffs: Mistakes are caught by the compiler while coding
Types are not checked at runtime, so stored data from older versions could still be invalid
evidence: types.ts defines 27 interfaces and a UserRole enum
